opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly I don't think there's one right answer. Granularity is partly a choice you make depending on what you want to explain.

The way I think about it: a good decomposition should let you describe the network's behavior with as few components as possible, while each component stays simple and faithful to what the network is actually computing. There's a tension there. If you go very coarse, say treating whole layers or attention heads as your units, each unit ends up doing lots of unrelated things. You get polysemanticity at the level of your components, and your explanations get messy. If you go very fine, down to individual parameters or ever-smaller features, you can split one coherent mechanism across many pieces, and you lose the sense that you've found something meaningful.

So the criterion I keep returning to is something like minimum description length. You want the decomposition that compresses the network's computation best. You can reconstruct the network's behavior faithfully, any given input only needs a small number of components active, and each component is as simple as it can be. In our work on parameter decomposition, we try to make those pressures explicit in the training objective. You have a faithfulness term, a term encouraging few components to be active on any input, and a simplicity term. Where those pressures balance tells you something about the natural grain of the computation.

That said, I don't think there's a single privileged level. Networks seem to have something like hierarchical structure. There are fine-grained mechanisms that compose into bigger ones. In practice you might want different resolutions for different questions. If you're auditing for a specific dangerous capability, you might want something coarser that captures the whole circuit. If you're trying to understand exactly how a model does some piece of arithmetic, you might want to zoom right in.

One thing I'd caution against is treating whatever comes out of your method at a given hyperparameter setting, like a dictionary size in sparse autoencoders, as the ground truth. We've seen with SAEs that features split as you scale the dictionary, and that tells you the granularity was partly an artifact of the method rather than a property of the network. That's part of why I've become more excited about decomposing parameters rather than activations. The mechanisms live in the weights. If you can find components that are actually the units the network uses to compute, the granularity question becomes more principled. You're asking what the smallest set of simple mechanisms is that together explain what the network does.

r001.rationale: The response says a good decomposition describes network behavior with as few components as possible while remaining faithful, and frames this as finding the smallest set of mechanisms that explains what the network does.

r002.rationale: It discusses faithfulness and reconstruction, but does not say that worsening reconstruction loss signals decomposition should stop or is inappropriate.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss subcomponent causal-importance scores or prefer scores near zero or one.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is honestly one of the central questions, and I don't think there's a single right answer, because the level of granularity you want depends on what you're trying to explain. If you're asking "why did the model output this token," you probably want a fairly coarse description. If you're asking "is there a mechanism inside this network that's tracking whether it's being evaluated," you need something finer, something that actually lines up with the computational structure the network is using.

The way I've come to think about it is that the network itself should tell you what the right granularity is. What you don't want to do is impose a decomposition from the outside, where you say, "okay, neurons are the unit," or "attention heads are the unit," or even "sparse dictionary features are the unit," and then just hope that the network's computation respects those boundaries. Often it doesn't. Neurons are famously polysemantic. Attention heads sometimes do several things at once. And with sparse autoencoders, you get this frustrating thing where if you make the dictionary bigger, features split into finer features, and if you make it smaller they merge, and it's not obvious which of those is the "real" description. The granularity ends up being a hyperparameter you chose rather than something you discovered.

So the criterion I'd actually use is something like: a component should be a part of the network that does one thing, in the sense that you can't break it into smaller pieces that each do something separately. If you can split a component into two parts that are each independently used for different functions, then you were at too coarse a level. And conversely, if two things always fire together and always get used together, splitting them apart isn't buying you any explanatory power; you've just added more pieces to your story for no benefit. So there's a kind of minimality at both ends: as few components as you can get away with, each as simple as it can be, while still faithfully reproducing what the network does.

And I'd emphasize that "faithfully reproducing what the network does" has to mean the mechanism, not just the behavior. You could get a decomposition that gives you the right outputs but where the pieces don't correspond to how the network actually computes them, and that's a trap. This is why I'm increasingly attracted to decomposing in parameter space rather than activation space. The parameters are the thing that actually implements the function. If you decompose the weights into pieces, you can then ask, for any given input, which pieces were causally necessary to produce the output, and you can make the decomposition lose as little as possible. That gives you a more principled handle on granularity than "what sparsity coefficient did I pick."

The honest caveat is that we're still at the stage where this is more of a research direction than a solved thing. In practice there's a bit of taste involved. You look at a decomposition and ask: do these components have interpretable stories, do they compose in sensible ways, does intervening on them do what I'd predict? If the answer is yes across a range of inputs, you're probably at roughly the right level. If you're constantly finding that a component does three different unrelated things, or that you need twenty components to explain something that should be one mechanism, that's the network telling you you've got the granularity wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says to use as few components as possible while keeping each simple and faithfully explaining the network’s computation, with granularity chosen for the explanation goal.

r002.rationale: It mentions minimizing decomposition loss, but does not say that worsening reconstruction loss signals that further decomposition may be inappropriate.

r003.rationale: It discusses causal necessity of components, but does not express a preference for causal-importance scores near zero or one rather than fractional.

astra-6.text:
I think the right level of granularity depends on what you’re trying to explain. You could decompose a network into individual neurons, but there’s no guarantee that a neuron corresponds to a single meaningful concept. Equally, you could treat a whole layer as a component, but then you’re probably hiding a lot of the interesting computation inside it.

So I’d look for a decomposition where the components have reasonably coherent functions, and where their interactions help explain the behavior we care about. Ideally, that explanation makes predictions: if we intervene on a component, does the network change in the way we expected?

There’s a tradeoff here. A finer decomposition gives you more detail, but it can also leave you with so many pieces that you haven’t really made the system easier to understand. A coarser decomposition is easier to reason about, but might miss important distinctions. I don’t think we should expect one privileged level that works for every question. We probably need multiple levels of abstraction, with some way of connecting them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing detail against interpretability and choosing a level based on the question, but does not state that the decomposition should use the fewest components needed to explain a specified level of functionality.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reconstruction loss or use worsening reconstruction as a signal to stop increasing decomposition.

r003.rationale: The response mentions intervening on components, but does not discuss causal-importance scores or prefer scores near zero or one over fractional values.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right level of granularity depends on what you want to explain. You could describe a network in terms of individual neurons, but there’s no guarantee that a neuron corresponds to a meaningful concept. Equally, you could treat an entire layer as a component, but then you might hide a lot of the structure you care about.

What I’d like is a decomposition into components that have relatively coherent functions, where we can test those functions by intervening on them. If I think a component is doing something, can I change it and get the effect I predict? And does that explanation hold across different inputs, rather than just a few examples?

There probably isn’t one uniquely correct resolution. You might need a hierarchy: a fairly coarse description to understand the overall computation, and then finer decompositions when you want to understand how a particular part works. The useful question is whether the extra detail gives you more explanatory or predictive power.
